newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian stocks seen tumbling further.
newsitem.headline: Canadian stocks seen tumbling further.

text.p: Canadian stocks, which have fallen well below their all-time highs in the past week, are expected to tumble further this year as interest rate jitters take their toll on already shaky investor confidence.
"I think the correction I would look at would be about five to 10 percent from the peaks, said Subodh Kumar, market strategist at brokerage CIBC Wood Gundy Inc.
"I would think that we will have a weak market (through) the first half and then recovery in the second half of the year," Kumar added.

The bellwether 300 Composite Index of the Toronto Stock Exchange, Canada's biggest equities market, shed nearly one percent on Monday, bringing the overall loss to about 3.5 percent from the record high hit on March 11.
The index was down 12.94 on Tuesday tO 6141.60.
The correction follows a banner 1996 in which the TSE 300 rose 25.74 percent, almost matching the 26 percent rise in the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
The TSE 300 is up about four percent so far this year, but down from a previous year-to-date increase of 7.10 percent.
Traders are focused this week on Wednesday's scheduled release of U.S. consumer price data, which should paint a clearer picture of U.S. inflation.
Recent U.S. data gave mixed signals -- with strong retail sales and nonfarm payrolls data offset by lower than expected producer price numbers.
The Federal Open Market Committee meets on March 25 and there is a growing conviction among investors that the Fed may raise interest rates.
Technical analyst Joe Ismail said the TSE 300 Composite Index would likely correct seven percent to about 5950, then rebound as bargain-hunters stepped in.
He said the second leg of a "healthy" correction would take the index to 5680, with a third leg likely to cut it to 5250 before year end.
But Ismail said that did not constitute a bear market.
"You only tend to go into bear markets when interest rates begin to move significantly higher. This is a corrective level, which is normal after six or seven years of an uptrend," Ismail said.
"That's nothing to get concerned about. Even 20 percent is still normal after six to seven years of an uptrend."
Trading has been increasingly volatile recently and analysts believed that would likely continue until the correction was over.
The past two weeks have been a roller coaster ride, propelled by testimony from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan in which he said caution was warranted given current equity market levels.
He added that interest rate increases may be necessary to pre-empt inflation in the United States, a statement that sent tremors through bond markets.
The TSE 300 hit 6116 on March 3 after several days of selling, its lowest level since mid-February.

But on March 5, in his second day of semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before Congress, Greenspan appeared to step back from his warning. He said stock market levels were reasonable if all corporate earnings forecasts proved correct.
That prompted a rally as soothed investors piled back into the market.
The sigh of relief sent the TSE 300 on an extended climb to a lifetime peak of 6348.02 on March 11.
